rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while ensuring strongly retained compounds elute. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to measure slope sensitivity of the crowded early cluster and the marginal later pair. This should reveal whether a shallower gradient improves selectivity enough to justify its time cost.

The early cluster responds to slope, but lengthening the gradient introduces a time penalty before resolving it. Test higher temperature at the original slope to seek better selectivity while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Retain the favorable high-temperature selectivity and make the gradient shallower to improve the sole unresolved pair. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, leaving a chance to reach the maximum CRF.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so temperature is the next selectivity lever. Testing 55 C may balance separation across the early three-peak cluster while retaining a comfortable margin below 10 minutes.

Return to 60 C and shift the starting composition upward to change selectivity in the early cluster. This tests a different solvent window because simply making the gradient shallower did not improve the limiting pair.
Injection 6 reached the maximum CRF; keep it as the benchmark and shorten the gradient by one step. This tests whether full resolution can be retained with an earlier last peak.

Narrow the gradient window to recover the small resolution deficit at eight minutes. The last peak previously eluted near 0.64 organic, so an endpoint of 0.85 should keep all peaks within the gradient while providing a shallower slope.

Injection 8 retains maximum CRF with an earlier last peak than injection 6. Raise the starting organic fraction one step to test further time savings, while checking whether the early cluster remains fully resolved.

Return to the better starting composition and test a six-minute gradient with a slope between injections 7 and 8. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, and this small slope increase may shorten the run while preserving full resolution.

Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; injection 10 has a small deficit despite its rounded CRF. Test the low-temperature selectivity regime to see whether a different ordering of the early cluster permits a faster fully resolved gradient.

Return to the favorable 60 C selectivity and lower the endpoint one step from injection 10 to recover its small resolution deficit. The last peak should still elute near the end of the gradient, giving a compact method with full resolution.

With maximum CRF already achieved, test a slightly shallower gradient for a larger resolution margin in the early cluster. This should retain a last-peak time comfortably below 10 minutes while making the separation less borderline.

At phi0 0.20, only one early pair remained unresolved; test a shallower slope to recover that separation while preserving the improved separation of its neighbor. The endpoint should remain high enough for all compounds to elute within 10 minutes.

Test whether a small temperature reduction improves the limiting early pair at the higher starting composition. Comparing directly with injection 9 will show whether temperature can support a faster fully resolved alternative to injection 8.

Return to the best starting composition and temperature, with an endpoint midway between injections 8 and 13. This should retain maximum CRF with more resolution margin than injection 8 and a shorter elution time than injection 13.

Maximum CRF is already secured, so test whether a shallower gradient provides a stronger resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Compare directly with injection 13 to quantify the remaining resolution–time tradeoff.

Lower the endpoint one step from injection 14 to address its sole remaining resolution deficit of R = 1.47. This tests whether the higher starting composition can achieve full resolution while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method. Test the unmeasured starting fraction of 0.10 at the same endpoint and duration to check whether selectivity improves enough to support further gradient shortening.

Preserve injection 8’s successful gradient slope but end the ramp after four minutes, testing a shorter programmed gradient. The last compounds will elute during the hold, so their retention and resolution will determine whether this compact program retains maximum CRF.

Raise the endpoint relative to injection 20 to reduce the late peak’s hold-related delay, while using the successful slope from injection 13. This should preserve full resolution with a six-minute programmed gradient and a last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Shorten elution relative to injection 17 by raising the endpoint one step pair of grid increments, while retaining a shallower slope than injection 8. This should preserve maximum CRF with a larger critical-pair resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved method.

Refine between the fully resolved methods from injections 6 and 22, aiming to shorten injection 22 while retaining a larger resolution margin than injection 8. Maximum CRF is already secured, and this nearby method should preserve it without a time penalty.

Use a slope close to injection 22’s fully resolved separation, but finish the programmed gradient two minutes earlier. All peaks should remain within the gradient, preserving maximum CRF and a critical-pair resolution near 1.6.

Use the final injection to test an untried method between injections 17 and 22, both fully resolved with no time penalty. It should retain maximum CRF with a critical-pair resolution near 1.6; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
